action_criteria.rationale: Orthostatic blood pressure on active standing is part of the initial evaluation of every transient loss of consciousness (ESC 2018 Class I); it tests orthostatic hypotension, the competing cause, before a cardiac cause is accepted.

general.query: syncope initial evaluation and risk stratification

results.key_finding: Initial evaluation comprises history, physical examination including supine and standing blood pressure, and a 12-lead ECG. High-risk features (syncope during exertion or supine, palpitations before the event, known structural or coronary disease, family history of sudden death under 40, high-risk ECG findings) call for early in-hospital evaluation with immediate ECG monitoring. Echocardiography is indicated when structural heart disease is known or suspected; EEG, brain imaging and routine laboratory panels are not recommended without a specific indication.
results.title: 2018 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope (Brignole M et al., Eur Heart J 2018;39:1883-1948)

results.key_finding: Risk stratification at the initial evaluation separates patients needing in-hospital monitoring and cardiac testing from those suitable for outpatient evaluation; targeted rather than routine blood testing is advised.
results.title: 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the evaluation and management of patients with syncope (Shen WK et al.)

general.summary: Guidelines base syncope work-up on the initial evaluation (history, examination, orthostatic BP, 12-lead ECG) and risk stratification; high-risk patients receive in-hospital ECG monitoring and targeted cardiac testing.

clinical_pearls: Sick sinus syndrome frequently presents with a normal or near-normal resting ECG between paroxysmal events; diagnosis requires ambulatory monitoring
The tachy-brady syndrome (paroxysmal AF followed by post-conversion sinus arrest) is a classic SSS variant that can be missed on a single ECG snapshot
Dual rate-control therapy with a beta-blocker and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker potentiates sinus node suppression and can unmask or worsen underlying sinus node dysfunction
Symptomatic bradycardia-tachycardia syndrome is a Class I pacing indication, because pacing allows the rate-control drugs to continue (ESC 2021)
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Four required actions (ECG, TTE, monitoring, review of the rate-slowing drugs); single diagnostic chain in which monitoring captures the symptom-correlated pause; the nuance is that a near-normal resting ECG does not exclude paroxysmal sinus node dysfunction.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Eleanor Marsh is a 74-year-old woman with a history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (on metoprolol and diltiazem for rate control), hypertension, and hypothyroidism who was brought to the emergency department by her daughter after a witnessed syncopal episode at home. Her daughter reports that her mother was standing in the kitchen preparing tea at approximately 8:40 AM when she abruptly went pale, slumped against the counter, and slid to the floor onto her left side without striking her head. She was unresponsive for approximately 12 to 15 seconds. Her eyes were closed and she appeared limp, with no tonic stiffening, no rhythmic limb jerking, and no facial twitching. She regained consciousness spontaneously, was immediately coherent and oriented, and asked what had happened. She had no confusion, no headache, and no post-event drowsiness. There was no tongue biting and no urinary or fecal incontinence. The patient herself recalls feeling entirely well moments before, with no preceding chest pain, palpitations, or shortness of breath. She does recall a brief fleeting sensation of lightheadedness and graying of her peripheral vision for approximately 2 to 3 seconds immediately before losing consciousness. Over the past six to eight weeks she has experienced three prior near-syncopal spells, each lasting a few seconds, during which her vision grayed and she felt as though she was about to black out, but she did not fall. These episodes have occurred both at rest and with mild exertion such as rising from a chair. She has also noticed increased fatigue and occasional palpitations, which she attributes to her known atrial fibrillation. She has had no fever, recent illness, vomiting, or diarrhea. She denies chest pain at rest, dyspnea, or lower extremity swelling. Her most recent thyroid check approximately eight months ago was reported as within normal limits. She has been on dual rate-control therapy with both metoprolol and diltiazem for approximately 18 months, started after her AF was perceived to be difficult to control with metoprolol alone. Her last cardiology visit was approximately one year ago and she had been doing well until the recent spells began.
